speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I first thank the opposition for doing me the honour of finding me important enough to inaugurate the proceedings on the discussion of departmental estimates in the House of Commons. The members of our party are very happy to be able to take part in the debate, and as you can see, Mr. Chairman, many of them are here to ask questions because they know the administration of the country is in good hands.
This is debatable.

We have hardly launched the debate and already the opposition is on the defensive.

Mr. Chairman, the control of government expenditures is not an easy task. Everybody is in favour of as much restraint as possible, but not a day goes by in the House without opposition members, who claim we spend too much, rising and calling for further outlays. That is why I welcome this opportunity of defending the government spending program before the House and not before a committee.
I am happy to report to the House that, true, there are internal administration problems, but the Canadian people are confident that we can solve them. The Canadian people know full well that if the Opposition were on this side of the House, it would be a disaster.
A year ago yesterday, the Opposition defeated us in the House of Commons and is still regretting it. The New Democratic Party no longer exists, it has no leader, it may have a new one soon who will perhaps devote three or four days to his responsibilities, provided he can listen to Brahms during the week-end. The Social Credit Party of Canada is faced with all kinds of problems, and the Progressive Conservatives have two or three leaders for the time being but none for the future.
So, Mr. Chairman, you can see why we are very much at ease today to defend our estimates in the House of Commons.
Over the last nine months, since I had the privilege of being appointed President of the Treasury Board, we have been faced with certain difficulties, and I would like to take a few minutes of the time of the House to deal with one problem concerning the general policy of the gouvern-ment; it is important for the Treasury Board in its expenditure policies, and for all Canadians, to realize that everyone of us, both in the House of Commons and outside, must face the facts.
Canada has been very lucky over the last 19 months since it was spared the economic recession our Southern neighbours, the United States, have been fighting over the last 18 months. Here in Canada, even though the economic expansion we wished for did not realize, we have been in a much better position than the United States, where recession has existed for 18 months now. Of course, we feel some of its effects, because we depend to a great extent on that giant neighbour by which so many of our resources are absorbed and with whom we do a great deal of trade.
Recently, Mr. Chairman, I had the pleasure to represent the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) at the special meeting of the Ministers of Finance of the OECD in Paris, and when I explained the situation in Canada, almost all my colleagues, ministers who were attending that conference, told me privately that while they admitted that we had some problems in Canada, they were all prepared, all those ministers of the OECD countries except perhaps one or two, to switch problems with us. Which means that our situation is not as difficult as it may appear to be.
Unfortunately, if we think that we have a ticket to absolute security, I feel we are simply deluding ourselves. That is why the Minister of Finance and members of the Cabinet initiated consultations throughout the country over the past months in order to encourage each and every Canadian to face the economic situation and to contribute
May 9, 1975

as much as possible to the bettering of our economic situation.
As for us, within the federal government, although things have been relatively peaceful for a long time in the field of collective agreements, we may have been experiencing more difficulties over the last few months. And we have sought to establish principles in order to clarify the situation.
That is why, for instance, we have said repeatedly over the last nine months that we intend to allow civil servants to keep the right to strike which was granted to them by Parliament in 1967, but on the other hand, we also said that in the case of all those who would defy the law and strike illegally, we would take legal action to have them abide by the law. Unfortunately, we have been forced to do so since the month of December against more than 2,000 civil servants.
If it takes as long to prosecute the longshoremen as it takes to prosecute the others, it will be a great success for the administration of justice in Canada!

Mr. Chairman, I am listening with interest to the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), but I am not the court. I have done my duty. I submitted the 2,000 cases to the Federal Government's Labour Relations Board, and from then on, it is up to the courts to decide. The chips are down. As far as I am concerned, I must say that the government has fulfilled its obligations. If the legislation is not sufficiently expeditious, if the machinery proves too slow, the Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons studying the Finkelman report may submit recommendations. We, as members of the government, have committed ourselves to table legislation following the submission of the Finkelman report, once the hon. members and senators will have made their recommendations to the government. But considering the legislation as it now stands, I feel, Mr. Chairman, that we have done what our duty called for us to do.
During the years 1971, 1972, 1973 and 1974, governmental expenses may have been considerable, I agree. Of course, in general, the Progressive Conservatives say that we spend too much. However, the New Democrats say that we do not spend enough. But the Canadian people recognize that we always have a much more balanced judgment in these situations and we do not fall into one extreme or the other.
In view of the inflationary pressures on the Canadian economy at this time, and in view of the increase of the unemployment rate in Canada, which is regrettable, but which can give us some satisfaction if we compare it to the rate in the United States since traditionally, during the winter, the United States always have 1 or 1.5 per cent less unemployed than Canada, during the last winter, despite the two metres of snow that we had, our unemployment rate was lower by nearly 2 per cent than that of the United States. However, in view of the delicate situation of our economy, we decided to control our expenses and we hope limit to 16 per cent the increase of our expenditures from 1974-75 to 1975-76. This is the policy that we have established and, since the beginning of this fiscal year, we
Business of Supply
believe that we can achieve this goal, but I must say, because it is important, that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) may soon present a new budget and, if he discovers any change in the economic situation of Canada following his present analysis, I shall have to adjust this prediction on the basis of any possible change in our economic policy.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that up till now, even though we have had many problems, we have coped with them in a much better way than most other countries, and I hope that the hon. members will make positive contributions when examining these estimates because, by its nature, my department is involved in the operations of all the other departments. I would like for once to see the Progressive Conservatives stand up and say where they would like us to cut down on our expenses. They always talk in a general way.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe is very good at that.
Yes.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. Would the minister try to stay with the facts? The procedure we have now is not new; it is almost as old as parliament. We lost the old rules by closure imposed by this government, but the minister's memory is so short

May 9, 1975
Business of Supply
that I thought I had better remind him before he got himself in trouble.
Mr. Chairman, I feel very humble when I receive advice from the hon. member. I am glad he has given me the opportunity, but perhaps I should sit down if he is hurt too much.
It doesn't bother me; I just turn up my collar and let the blizzard blow.
We will remember this speech on budget night.
I think I will sit down now. I welcome-
Hear, hear!

I can tell the hon. member for Edmonton Centre that I will be here at five o'clock. I have the right to reply to everyone, and I will enjoy that time. I am not going into a back-room; I will hear the questions and reply to them. I hope I will be invited again, because I enjoy these occasions.

Mr. Chairman, I wish the President of the Treasury Board had explained, in the 20 minutes allotted to him, some of the inconsistencies in the estimates now before us, not only within his department but in other departments of which he has over-all control. Instead, we have been subjected to some type of verbal biomass.
I believe that the essence of committee of the whole procedure is to get the facts. I notice that the minister adopted the trick of the government in talking about other jurisdictions and stating that somehow there are other countries that are doing even worse than we are. This is not in accordance with the facts. I think we should get that on the record at the beginning of this debate.
I find it very interesting that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have suddenly discovered that somehow the average worker in Canada is losing his productivity in relation to the United States. They must have known this at least a year ago, but they failed to reveal it to the Canadian public. The April 19, 1975, monthly economic letter put out by the First National City Bank of New York compared the competitive position of various countries with that of the United States. I think this government has a tremendous amount to answer for. The comparison shows that in 1965 the unit labour cost of Canadian production in relation to the United States was 85 per cent, and by 1970 it was still 85 per cent. That is when the Minister of Finance and his predecessor, and the President of the Treasury Board and his predecessor, started to tamper with things.
We find that by 1973 the productivity percentage had risen, in terms of Canadian productivity to that of the United States, to 96 per cent. Did any minister at that time point out that we were losing our productivity in relation to the United States? No, Mr. Chairman. At the end of 1974 our productivity was up to 99 per cent of that of the United States. That is one of the things the government should be more candid about with the Canadian people.
Look at it another way. How often have we heard people boast that we are the second wealthiest nation in the 
world. Actually, we are no longer the second wealthiest nation, per capita: we now rank sixth, behind such countries as Switzerland, Sweden, Denmark, the United States and Kuwait. The last named country jumped ahead, of course, because of its huge oil revenues. Canada has slipped, largely because there has been too much public sector interference with the private sector. There has been too much government and too much Treasury Board spending in the past.
The minister said he looks forward to answering each participant in the debate. I hope he is making notes because I want him to answer some questions. For example, why did estimates of $22.4 billion in 1973 jump to $28.7 billion in 1974? That represents a spending increase of $6.3 billion. The minister admits that this is so and suggests he will try to do better next year. By that, the minister means that our annual increase in spending will not be 25 per cent but 16 per cent. If all federal government spending in the first 77 years after Confederation, from 1867 to 1944, were added together-and bear in mind that spending in two world wars must be included-the total would be $27.8 billion, which is less than the federal government spent in 1974 alone.
What does that mean?
You don't know?

How typical of a government supporter to ask what that means. At one time governments were concerned even about $1 million; now the government appears to be unconcerned about the spending of $28 billion and more.
It's just the taxpayers' money; that's all.

Let me put the figures in perspective. Federal government expenditures for 1974 were twice the size of expenditures for 1969, three times the size of 1961 expenditures, and more than 12 times the size of 1950 expenditures. If expenditures continue increasing at the rate they increased between 1973 and 1974, they will double in less than three years. I suggest that members of the House ought to be concerned because government spending is out of control.
Hear, hear!

Since 1968, that unfortunate year when the Prime Minister took power, federal government expenditures have increased by 134.8 per cent, but the average weekly wage has gone up barely 100 per cent. As you know, the federal government in 1974 spent $28.7 billion. Let me bring that spending into perspective. This represents daily spending of $78.7 million, hourly spending of $3.3 million and, taking it down to the minute, $54,600 every minute. That is how fast the government spends the taxpayers' money. If you want to know why, consider the number of civil servants employed. The President of the Treasury Board has the nerve to say that he is doing a
May 9, 1975

good job containing the numbers employed in the civil service.
He said he is just learning.

I wish he would learn a little better, because despite the computer age in which we live we employ proportionately more civil servants today than ever before in our history. In the last four years the increase has been significant. There was one civil servant employed in 1970 for every 78 Canadians; in 1974 there was one civil servant for every 67 Canadians.
The great advantage of committee of the whole procedure is that it gives us the opportunity to question the minister on various aspects of his estimates. I hope government supporters will not start their sandbagging tactics, as they often do in standing committees, as I think it is in the public interest that the minister should be asked questions directly. Hopefully, he will give direct answers. The minister said that he hopes to contain spending this year to a 16 per cent increase. What are his intentions for future years? Is spending to increase next year by 14 per cent, 12 per cent, or 10 per cent? In short, will he adhere to guidelines the government is asking others in the economy to follow?
He is going to use his Ouija board.

If the government is allowed to increase spending by even 16 per cent per year, cumulative government spending will increase by 110 per cent in five years. An increase of 16 per cent is extravagant. Therefore, when the government says it hopes to hold its spending to about 16 per cent more, that is totally unacceptable.
Especially when the gross national product goes up only 3 per cent.

As the minister keeps talking about restraint, I think he should explain why it is necessary for his department to be housed in such luxurious quarters in Place Bell Canada. I think all members of the House should look at those quarters, and the conditions under which the minister and his staff are working. They will see palm trees, Australian umbrella tree-
Swimming pools.
-split-leaf philodendrons, and all the rest of it. I think they will agree that the quarters are lavish.
Beyond extravagance.
The Treasury Board is operating in quarters which would do justice to a tropical botanical garden.
It is a lotus land.
Take a look at it: it is a paradise.
But not compared with some of the homes in your riding.
Oh, oh!

In the standing committee I tried to obtain details as to what the department is paying for these
Business of Supply
luxurious quarters. What is the rent per square foot? What did all the tapestries, beautiful shrubs, desks and other luxurious appointments cost? This is one of the most luxurious suites one can see in Ottawa.
If not in Canada.
I was told that information would be supplied, but so far it has not been and I trust the minister will supply it without further delay.

Mr. Chairman, I can give the hon. member that information right away. Treasury Board has
220,000	square feet on five floors in Place Bell Canada. The rent was negotiated by DPW at $5.97 per square foot.
And how many palm trees and split-leaf philodendrons are there?

Mr. Chairman, that is precisely the point I was making. The department is renting 220,000 square feet at more than $5 per square foot. Why, that is the equivalent of almost four acres of land at more than $5 per square foot. If you add what the Department of Finance has in the same luxurious building, you find they have almost ten acres of space that they are renting at approximately $5 per square foot.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: That is shameful.
My colleagues tell me it is almost five acres of space that they are renting. Let me put it in another context. Five dollars per square foot, times 220,000 means $1,100,000 for rental space alone.
Shame!
It costs almost $100,000 a month to house the minister and his entourage-and this is the minister who has the nerve to talk to Canadians about restraint.
Hear, hear!

If the minister wants to give us some information, he can tell us the price of some of the furniture in his palatial offices. What did it cost for the wall-hangings, plants and the botanical niceties he apparently feels is necessary?
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. The President of the Treasury Board has not bought one chair since taking over these offices for the department.
Hear, hear!
Did you ever see such irresponsibility on the part of the government?
The hon. member was not telling the truth.

Here we have the minister, sitting four seats away from his predecessor, and he has the nerve to suggest that whatever furnishings he is enjoying at the present time have nothing to do with him. We are talking

Business of Supply
about the fact that the government has housed the Treasury Board in extremely extravagant space and then turns around and tells the civil servants, wage earners and taxpayers of this nation to use restraint. In the standing committee I asked the minister to supply us with the cost of furnishings, carpets and all the rest of it for the 220,000 square feet being rented in Place Bell Canada. speechtext: Order, please. The Chair has ruled on the procedure to be followed in committee of the whole. The questions will be put, and they can be answered following the time that has been allotted to the hon. member.

To be explicit, Mr. Chairman, I have -eferred to the 16 per cent target the minister feels they hope to restrain themselves to within the current year. In answering the points I have raised, I would like the minister to specifically indicate the following. First, does he believe that the 16 per cent will be attained in the current year? Second, what does he see for each of the subsequent years 1977, 1978, 1979 and 1980? If this government is going

to attempt to work out a consensus arrangement with other sectors of the economy, surely they have to state at what level they are willing to restrain government spending.
The document that was tabled yesterday was very clear. As far as labour is concerned, they are spelling it out. They believe labour must systematically cut their increases to roughly 8 per cent per annum. Does the President of the Treasury Board have a similar program to ensure that government spending will fall by a certain percentage each year over the next five years, assuming that this restraint program comes into position?
We should also have an indication from the President of the Treasury Board as to the mechanics within the department while working out the spending programs of government. I understand that at the present time they are considering the 1977 estimates. Certain submissions have been made to the department. I believe the minister should outline the significance of budget A and budget B which are submitted in that process.
He should also indicate to what extent he has been overruled by his cabinet colleagues. For example, is it true that the family allowance program that was advanced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare did not go through Treasury Board until after it was agreed to by the cabinet? The fact is that these two ministers, who should in any cabinet be the watchdogs of the treasury and should insist that their colleagues restrain their spending, are not performing their job. This is why we have such high spending in this country and it is the reason the Canadian public is skeptical about any talk of consensus so far as restraint and an anti-inflation program is concerned. -I would like to make the point that we are dealing with one of the most important portfolios in the federal government. The Treasury Board is responsible for not just the $335 million listed in its own estimates; it is, in effect, responsible for the whole book because the estimates of all departments have to receive the approval of the Treasury Board.
In the process of doing its job, I suggest that the Treasury Board has an influence far beyond government itself. It has a commanding influence on the very make-up of Canadian society. I break this down, for the purpose of this short speech, to three headings: the Treasury Board is responsible for the spending policy of the federal government, it is also responsible for the wages and incomes policy of the federal government, and it is responsible for policies relating to pensions and other social benefits.
To the extent that the Treasury Board sets standards in these three areas-how we spend our money, what our incomes are, and what our pensions and other social benefits are-we are into the very heart of Canadian society itself, and I hope that for at least some of the afternoon the discussion will be on these serious matters rather than on the question of whether certain office chairs are covered with leather or suede.
Hear, hear!

I always enjoy listening to the President of the Treasury Board. I enjoyed meeting him when he first came here a dozen years ago. He was not quite the orator he is now, and, he did not know a word of English. Just listen to him now! He has come a long way.
Hear, hear!

He likes to say that the Tories across from him claim that he is spending too much money, while we down here in the NDP corner want to spend more. So he feels very comfortable being in the middle. May I point out to him that it is true that we criticize the Progressive Conservatives for having only one notion, namely, to cut down expenditure, but we do not-

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: That is not true.
That is not right.

Hon. members have had all the morning and they will have the rest of the afternoon. Let me have my 20 minutes. We are not just advocating the expenditure of more money; we are advocating proper priorities in government spending. We do not want to see money wasted on frills and non-essentials. We do not want to see our society given the kind of direction that results in overcapitalization in terms of filling stations, office buildings and an undersupply of homes, health services and the other things that our people need. Therefore, I say we are deeply concerned about the activities of this department because it not only determines how government money will be spent, but it 
sets the pattern for the spending of Canadians generally; and I argue very strongly that the kind of society we will have in the years immediately ahead and in the distant future depends on the kind of priorities that this department establishes.
I urge very strongly, therefore, that the Treasury Board think in these terms and realize that there is a point to our claim that the first charges on public money should be for the health, wellbeing and housing of our people; that public money should be spent to provide the jobs and services necessary to improve the quality of life in Canada.
So I say, let us not spend all afternoon on the question of whether so many dollars were spent on a particular office here or somewhere else. Let us have some discussion about priorities in our spending, knowing that in so doing we are determining the kind of Canada that we will have in the years that lie ahead. The President of the Treasury Board, a few weeks ago in the course of one of the labour disputes that was taking place, made the remark that he did not want the federal government to be a pace-setter. I suggest to him that, whether or not he wants the government to be a pace-setter, that is precisely what it is. The percentage of people who work for the federal government or Crown agencies is much higher than it used to be. This is the direction that we have pushed for, and we welcome it. The government is involved in so many of the activities of our country that the standards the government sets determine to a very large extent the standard of life- indeed, the quality of life-in Canada. So I say the priorities the Treasury Board establishes for the total expenditures of the government give a lead to the priorities of spending in Canada as a whole; and that makes our function at this moment terribly important.
The second heading I gave a few moments ago was wages and incomes policy. The Minister of Finance does a lot of talking about what wages should be paid and he talks about restraint on everybody except, of course, ourselves. But it is the President of the Treasury Board who, in very practical terms, has the final say about the wages and incomes of many thousands of persons, those in the employ of the federal government and, in turn, Crown corporations, and so on. I welcome the fact that we have established collective bargaining; and for all the aches and pains there may be in the process, it is alive and well and I hope it is here to stay. But there is one idea the government ought to start putting on the table when it comes to collective bargaining and I hope the President of the Treasury Board will take this to heart. I suggest that one of the reasons we are having so much trouble in the wages and incomes field in Canada is the growing spread between the incomes of those in lower brackets and those in upper brackets. I suggest that one of the myths we continue to subscribe to at the bargaining table is the myth of percentage increases. It sounds fine and plausible to say we should give a 10 per cent increase, but 10 per cent of $10,000 is $1,000 and 10 per cent of $40,000 is $4,000.
Hear, hear!

Very good.
May 9, 1975

My hon. friends approve of my arithmetic, but I suggest that this is not a laughing matter. This is one of the things happening in our day. We are assuming that to raise wages on a percentage basis, is the thing to do but the result is that we are getting increasingly wide discrepancies and when people in the middle or lower income groups see people in the upper income groups going higher and higher into the stratosphere, they want more, too-and that is the picture we have.
Tell that to the unions.

I am telling it to members of parliament. This House gave a lead to this country. Hon. members wanted a 50 per cent increase but toned it down to 33Vz per cent with 7 per cent escalation compounded on an annual basis. I suggest that if we want to give some leadership, it should start here. We made that decision or, rather, parliament made that decision. Some of us were strongly opposed to it, but I suggest to the President of the Treasury Board that in wage talks going on with those involved in collective bargaining and in the adjustments which are made in the upper reaches of the public service, it is time to start talking increases which are in lower percentages for those in the upper brackets but not for those in the lower brackets.
I do not know what will happen in terms of salaries for those at the top level, the deputy ministers, assistant deputy ministers and assistants to assistant deputy ministers-those in the $30,000, $40,000 and $50,000 bracket. I believe there is some kind of study being made about them and no doubt a report will be made discussing what has happened in the private sector, and so on, and setting it all out in percentage terms, and we are likely to receive another of those recommendations. Such a recommendation will do just as much damage to the wage situation in this country as has been done in this place and over in the Senate as well.
When one talks about the cost of living having gone up and the need for people to be compensated with higher wages to meet the rise in the cost of living, I suggest that that percentage increase should apply only to that portion of one's income which is actually spent meeting the cost of living, but because persons have enough to cover the cost of living and then more for luxuries is no reason why the percentage increase should apply both to the basic part and to that which is gravy on the top.
I make this speech on this occasion because although the President of the Treasury Board may not set all the wages in Canada, he has much to do, even in the collective bargaining process, with the wage levels in the public service, those which come under collective bargaining, and perhaps even still more to do with the wages and salaries of those in higher brackets who receive more. The strong plea I make to him is that he not live for ever by the myth that percentage increases solve the problem. Percentage increases are fine for those in the lower or middle-income brackets, but the same percentage increases given to those in the upper brackets simply cause more trouble.

Is the union movement agreeable to that?

My hon. friend asks a very good question. He wants to know whether the union movement is agreeable to that. There is real trouble in the union movement over that; I do not deny that for one moment. Those higher up still want to receive just the same percentage as those lower down. But someone has to give the lead somewhere. If my idea is sound, and there are many people in the union movement who agree with it, I think someone has to give a lead to it somewhere and I am hoping that the President of the Treasury Board will try to give that lead.
Explain your split-level cost of living percentages to some and not to others.
If my hon. friend is asking that I set a figure, I think by doing that I would simply start an argument over such a figure, and I do not feel like doing that. I want to stick to the principles.
Explain how it would work.

I think that if there has been an increase in the cost of living of, say, 10 per cent, wage increases should be 10 per cent of that portion or up to that level which is regarded as covering a standard, basic cost of living. For incomes above that point, the increase should be less than 10 per cent. Where incomes are way up, there should be none at all.
About 7 per cent?

My hon. friend had better just sit in his seat and keep quiet. That 7 per cent we are to get is compounded on top of 33'/3 per cent, so that by the end of this parliament we will be getting an increase of 62 or 63 per cent. I will move to the other heading I mentioned, that of pensions and social benefits. One is aware that old age security and other benefits in that area come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, but the President of the Treasury Board is responsible for pension policy as it affects public servants, the armed forces, RCMP personnel, and a whole host of others. We will receive the list in a few days when we deal with Bill C-52. I call upon the minister to straighten out some of the anomalies in that situation, little details such as the fact that armed forces personnel have to wait until age 60 before they get their escalation, and also the fact that the escalations are always behind, as applies in some other cases as well. There is also the need to increase the percentage paid to widows. But I mention this subject now because I think the principle I have suggested regarding wages and salaries will some day also have to apply to pensions.
I take some pride in having fought for about 25 years to have retired civil service pensions escalated. I remember the thrill it was when we finally won and the present

Minister of Public Works stood here one Friday afternoon and announced it, but I am disturbed by the fact that in one respect we won too well. The kind of percentage increase we now have is such that when in January of this year there was a 10 per cent increase in all public service pensions, that meant that the $2,000 people received an increase of $200, but those with $25,000 pensions received a $2,500 increase. I think the principle I have just been enunciating regarding the wages and incomes of our people should apply to pensions. In other words, I am arguing for us in Canada to move more in the direction of an egalitarian society. Perhaps it will take us a while to get there, but at least we can narrow the gap. You do not narrow the gap when you use the percentage formula and keep raising those at the top salary more than those at the bottom. You narrow the gap if you exercise restraint for those higher up and bring the others closer to them.
As I said earlier, I am arguing for this not just because it applies to many thousands in the public service or retired from the public service, but because what the President of the Treasury Board said the other day is the fact: he is a pace-setter. To the extent that we establish these ways of doing things in the public service, we establish them as a whole.
I am prepared to let my case rest at that for the moment. I call upon the House to treat this department as the serious one it is. The estimates of the Treasury Board itself are a little over 1 per cent of the total estimates in the book, but the Treasury Board approves all the estimates in the book and so is largely responsible for the social direction established in this country. I hope the President of the Treasury Board will pay some attention to the ideas I have submitted this afternoon.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to reply to the two points that the hon. member has raised. I must congratulate him on the level of his participation; he is much less concerned with the quality of furniture than with people. The hon. member spoke about wages and incomes policies and the influence that the Treasury Board has. I disagree with him, however, when he says that sometimes we become the pace-setter, because I have tried to avoid that. I have said many times that when I resist some demands as President of the Treasury Board, it is not just because it would be too expensive for the federal government to implement them. Of the $32 billion estimates in front of the House today, we spend only 14 per cent on wages, so even if I overspent my budget by 10 per cent it would be only 1.4 per cent of the total expenditure, which would not destroy the whole system.
It would be a very simple solution for me to become a pace-setter and to put pressure on all other levels of public and private administration, but I do not think we should use the federal government for that purpose. We have to maintain high standards and we cannot allow problems to develop that would affect other levels of government and the private sector. Our policy is comparability. We want our people to be as well paid, but not better paid, than other people.
Some hon. members complain to me because in Canada 20 per cent of the federal civil servants are on a regional

rate, and other members from places like Vancouver, the Yukon, or Seven Islands complain about the national rates because the cost of living is higher there. We try to pay blue collar workers, who are not too mobile, a rate comparable to that paid to the same type of worker in the same town because we feel we should not put a burden on the local economy by paying higher than our competitors in the same labour pool.
With a national rate, you end up with a situation like the strike of firefighters in Vancouver. They wanted the regional rate because they earn $2,000 a year less than the city of Vancouver firefighters. We wanted to pay them the same as the city, but the national rate did not permit us to do that and the unions do not permit us to do it either. We are negotiating those things with the unions now, winning some arguments and losing some. So, Mr. Chairman, I do not agree with the hon. member that we have to be the pace-setter. I think we should avoid that, but should treat our employees as well as anybody else on a comparable basis.
As far as the spread between the lower and the higher bracket is concerned, I think the hon. member has a good point. We have to avoid speaking in terms of percentage. The hon. member's arithmetic is simple and understandable-10 per cent of 10,000 is 1,000, and 10 per cent of 40,000 is 4,000. We have managed to narrow the gap to some extent in the last five years when we have given 8.7 per cent more to people in the operational, administrative, support and technical categories than for the people at the top level. That means the people who are lower than the SXs receive 8.7 per cent more than the higher echelon. It is not much of a difference, but it is a difference.
The hon. member argues that everyone should earn more or less the same salary, but I do not know any country where everyone is equal. I had a discussion with the ambassador to Canada of one of the socialist countries, and asked him the difference in pay between a minister and a plumber in his country. He said that the minister gets about five times more than the plumber. If a plumber in Canada makes $20,000, then I should be making $100,000, and I am very far away from that. Mr. Chairman, it is just a dream to think of everyone on the same level of pay. That dream has not been realized over the centuries and I do not think we are on the verge of realizing it in Canada or anywhere else.
The hon. member said that the government should intervene in society and try to correct some of the inequities. Just to show the increase in our expenditures, I should like to point out that in 1966-67 the federal government spent a little less than $2 billion on health and welfare; in 1974-75, we will spend more than $7 billion. In eight years, social and welfare expenditure has increased 314 times. Of course, all members of the House have been associated with that. When I came here in 1963 we did not have things like medicare. Old age pension payments were very low and were not indexed. We had no national hospitalization program, nor were there many of the social benefits which exist today in our society. We have quadrupled family allowances, and I am proud to have been associated with this.

That is the trend, but there is a limit. In our society, there are now fewer inequalities than existed, say, 25 years ago. Today you will see fewer people begging on the sidewalks. We do not see beggars any more and this is the result of legislation which members of this House have supported in the last 10 or 15 years. I think we should keep on this course. I know we cannot do everything in one parliament or in one generation, but I think most hon. members agree that the fabric of our society is stronger now and there is more social equality than there was 25 years ago. Of course, a lot remains to be done. We hope that if the economy grows sufficiently strong, we can do more. But we need time and more growth in our economy if we are to achieve our aims. I hope everyone will get the message and do their best to improve conditions in the land.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when I first listened to the minister this morning I wondered where I was. I have always understood that in committee of the whole ministers make submissions and that estimates are dealt with seriously. I admit that my practical experience is limited, but I have read about this procedure and we dealt with several matters earlier in the session in committee of the whole. Frankly, I was offended by the minister's attitude earlier today.
Some hort. Members: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: He has used this procedure which has been established in other parliaments and which, until 1968, was followed in this parliament for the purpose of getting his message across. The members of the committee and the public want to know, basically, how the government is managing the affairs of this country. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said, this matter must be treated with seriousness and not in a partisan way.
Oh, boy!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Earlier today I heard the hon. member for York-Simcoe direct a number of questions to the minister, not one of which, so far as I can remember, has been answered. Those questions dealt with furniture, office space and other matters. They were legitimate questions put to the government on behalf of the people of Canada and they have not been answered. The government should not treat committee of the whole procedure in the way the Prime Minister treats the question period. This is not the place to parry: this is the place where the government is to be held accountable for its spending, for its objectives and for the working of its policies.
Get to the point.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I will get to it in a
minute. The President of the Treasury Board says to those in the opposition who are asking questions, "Tell us what you would do." I say to the President of the Treasury Board, "My God, you won the election"-and I don't begrudge the victory, but in that election the people of Canada placed on the shoulders of the government certain
Business of Supply
responsibilities. One of them is to account to parliament and the people, and the other is to act.
And to govern.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
The minister spoke about the Canadian people having long faces. You bet they have long faces. We are discussing these estimates in a strange atmosphere, an atmosphere in which unemployment is increasing, inflation is escalating, senior citizens are falling ever further behind, housing starts are down, our balance of payments situation is in trouble and our dollar, according to rumours, may be devalued. The Minister of State responsible for housing cannot meet his optimistic expectations. Further, the optimism of the Minister of Finance of five months ago has evaporated. Yesterday he put on his red tie and grey suit and finally admitted that this country is in trouble.
That is the atmosphere in which we are asking the government to account. The President of the Treasury Board has a responsibility. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said-I do not always agree with him, but I agree with him on this-the Treasury Board is the heart and soul of the government's operation; its tentacles spread to every department. It has the responsibility to account and to establish priorities. I suggest that there is little evidence of priority planning on the part of that department of government.
More than that, Treasury Board has the responsibility of overseeing government programs. It should not hide expenditures, but disclose them. It should not refuse to give forecasts on unemployment and inflation, but give them to parliament and the Canadian people. That has not happened in this country. If we are to continue in committee of the whole with the kind of charade we witnessed before lunch, I do not hold out much hope for the continuation of this kind of procedure.
I hope that some backbench members on the government side are prepared to ask the kind of questions which we on this side of the House are asking. They, too, are private members and ought to be concerned about the workings of parliament. They, too, ought to be concerned about where this country is going, at what pace and what the benefits are to be. They, too, should ask how the government is to solve this or that problem; what we are to do about housing, for example. They, too, should question the President of the Treasury Board and not try to barrack those who are trying to question the minister in committee.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Sit down and go back to sleep. The Treasury Board has the responsibility to oversee the financial operations of this government and to see that rules concerning the spending of money are observed. It must see to it that cabinet ministers follow those rules in their spending. I say that is not happening in this country. It has not happened recently.
I directed a series of questions to the Minister of Labour, in his capacity as minister responsible for mul-ticulturalism, about a certain matter. On December 20, 1974, I asked the minister certain questions about a con-

May 9, 1975
Business of Supply
tract involving the sum of $250,000. The figure is not important; the principle is. I asked the minister why a certain contract had been awarded to Price, Rubin and Partners who are, coincidentally, the former law partners of the Minister of Labour.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order-on two points of order, actually. First, I submit the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton is going beyond the scope of these particular estimates by raising a matter to do with multiculturalism. Second, as the hon. member invited backbenchers of the governing party to pronounce themselves on certain matters, I suggest to him that they have not done so because none of them has been recognized by the Chair.
Order!
Hon. members here have tried to catch the attention of the Chair.
That is not a point of order. Pull in your horns.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Dealing with this matter, Mr. Chairman, that firm received three contracts without tenders during the fiscal year 1974-75. There was $170,000 provided to promote the efforts of the Department of the Secretary of State. That submission was signed by the Minister of Labour. There was $75,000 for an ethnic festival in Ottawa.
Mr. Chairman-
Why don't you sit down?

Perhaps the hon. member for Calgary North would like to take the chair and rule on this matter. I point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that I raised a point of order, namely, that the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton is attempting to deal with the Department of the Secretary of State. I suggest he ought not be allowed to do that.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. If the hon. member will look at vote 1 of the Treasury Board, he will see that the hon. member is in fact in order.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
The last one was $250,000 to publicize the aims of several departments and cultural agencies, launched in the winter of 1974. That submission was signed by the Minister of Labour on November 21, 1974.
I am not going to deal with the question of the commission that was received by that particular department because in terms of the amount I understand the commission was reasonable. However, it is a fact that under the rules of the watchdog, Treasury Board, its approval must be sought for all ad expenditures exceeding $10,000 before commitments are made. The fact is the ads in this campaign for a quarter of a million dollars appeared in the papers well before January 16, 1974. This is the information I tried to get from the Minister of Labour without success. I questioned the President of the Treasury Board

as well. Treasury Board did not give final approval until January 16, 1975. The Minister of Labour admitted that in a letter he wrote to me on April 9. He said there was a Treasury Board document to cover it dated November 21, 1974, but the fact is the money was spent on this contract well before Treasury Board approval was received. I believe, and will continue to believe unless I am advised to the contrary, that was an attempt to cover up this kind of program which has been going on for a long time.
I am also advised that Mr. Price of Price, Rubin and Partners stated that he was not aware he needed Treasury Board approval before work could proceed. I do not know how he could be unaware of that. I am not going to make any comment with regard to the connections between the Minister of Labour and Mr. Price who heads that department. I have said all I want to say. However, out of this litany of difficulty there are a few questions I want to put to the President of the Treasury Board. This is only exemplary of a number of things that the government has been doing, even if it is well intentioned.
What procedure did the Treasury Board follow when Price, Rubin and Partners, Inc. were recommended for the $250,000 contract? Would the minister explain what procedure is followed by the government which enables individuals or firms to be granted government contracts without tenders being called? Does the minister not agree that the granting of government contracts without tenders being called smacks of political patronage, and that legislation should be introduced to prohibit this from occurring in the future?

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. I understand that the order for today is to study votes Nos. 1, 5, 10 and 20 of the Treasury Board. I have looked at those votes. None of them covers any of the matters which have been brought to the attention of the government by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please.
I am on a question of privilege and I would like to complete my point.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. Whether it is on a point of order or a question of privilege, the Chair has ruled on the matter which disturbs the hon. member for Nipissing. To repeat, vote No. 1 concerns those matters which come under the administrative authority of the Treasury Board. This is a broad category dealing with a large number of policy matters under the jurisdiction of the government. The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton is quite in order in his remarks.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will begin by repeating the question I tried to put before I was interrupted. Does the minister not agree that the granting of government contracts without tenders being called smacks of political patronage, and that legislation should be introduced to prohibit this from occurring in the future? Is that not a reasonable proposition?
Will the minister explain why Price, Rubin and Partners, Inc. proceeded with their multiculturalism campaign before the Treasury Board approved this contract? Is this standard procedure for all government contracts or just
May 9, 1975

those which are granted without tenders being called? Will the minister explain why Price, Rubin and Partners, Inc. were not informed that they must seek Treasury Board approval before their work could proceed? In light of Mr. Price's statements that he was not aware that he needed Treasury Board approval, is this House to assume that work was started on the two previous contracts before they were approved by the Treasury Board?
I think there is something to be answered for here, and this is only with regard to one minister, albeit in a relatively small monetary area of government expenditures. However, in terms of the principle of accountability and the integrity of Treasury Board, and indeed of the President of the Treasury Board, what discretion do ministers have to spend money? How is it being used? These are legitimate questions to be put to any President of the Treasury Board in the course of this kind of proceeding.
I think the hon. member for Nipissing would be well advised to sit back and listen rather than interrupt on questions of privilege. The answer may well be that there is innocence.
I doubt it.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
There may be some who doubt that. I can forgive them if they do. However, regardless of what might be said, I think these questions are legitimate and should be answered.
There is another question I want the President of the Treasury Board to answer. Will he consider, or in fact review all government contracts which the Minister of Labour has approved for similar irregularities and, if they exist, report to this House? I think that is a legitimate request. At the same time, he might ask his brothers in the ministry to do the same. I think this is quite legitimate in view of this kind of matter occurring.
As I understand it, the purpose of committee of the whole is to deal with the whole issue of accountability in parliamentary government. The estimates must be accountable as well. They must stand up to scrutiny. I have been going into this matter. I will mention certain estimates.
It is a fact that the estimates for the official languages branch are down 48 per cent although authorized manhours, according to the same estimates, are the same. In an age when the government, following its policy, is promoting the use of two official languages, expanding schools and hiring teachers, the estimates of the official languages branch are somehow down. Do you know what this suggests to me, Mr. Chairman? It suggests that if the true cost of the program were known, however well intentioned the expenditure might be, the people of Canada would shake in their beds. I ask the President of the Treasury Board to produce the figures. They are scattered, now, through all the departments. It is important that he should produce them.
The Official Languages Act embodies a principle which was supported by all parties in the House, but there is a difference of opinion as to the manner in which it is being implemented in the public service. Surely, these items
Business of Supply
should be brought together. How much is this program costing? Are the Canadian people getting dollar value for the tremendous amount being spent?
I ask this question in the light of another revelation. Here is the document which was produced to the Director of Finance and Administration and the Director of Planning and Evaluation by the personnel adviser of a certain department of government. It said:
For the third consecutive year, the Commissioner of Official Languages has reported to cabinet that in general the public service is not meeting the requirements of the Official Languages Act.
In February of this year, the Prime Minister met with the deputy heads of all government departments and agencies and indicated that the Public Service was not making sufficiently rapid progress toward the attainment of the objective of institutional bilingualism and that the bilingualism process must be accelerated.
What have they done? They have decided that term employees who fill designated bilingual positions for six months or more must be bilingual at the time of selection. Not only is this stupid in terms of policy but it is discriminatory. In effect, it is saying that those who want to work for the government on a term basis in a position which is designated bilingual must be bilingual from the outset. Nobody quarrels with the principle of the Official Languages Act, but it is this kind of nonsense which arouses the ire of Canadians. Indeed, it is this kind of nonsense which prompts me to ask: how much is this program costing? I think this is a legitimate question for one to ask, especially in this committee where the government is supposed to account for such matters.
The minister might not be able to answer all these questions immediately and if that is the case I am prepared to see the answers tabled. Preferably, I should like to have the answers now, because if this procedure in the committee of the whole is to mean anything these are questions to which answers should be forthcoming.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I cannot reply to the questions at this moment because each time I get up to reply another member of the House is deprived of an opportunity to speak. If my speaking has the effect of depriving another hon. member from asking questions I prefer to remain in my seat.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Laurier.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, this arises from the position the minister is taking. While the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton was speaking, several meetings were going on across the way. In fact, there was louder talk over there than I could hear from this side of the chamber. Now the minister says he wants to let everybody speak. Mr. Chairman, I saw the Liberal whip going around among the members of his party. They are going to talk, and we shall get no answers. This whole procedure will be a farce unless we can get information.
This morning I reminded hon. members that the opposition had enjoyed certain well established rights, ever since confederation, when it came to voting supply. I might have added that in the old days we would say to a minister, "We are not going to pass your estimates until we get answers to our questions." But under this hanky-panky compromise in which we find ourselves today the minister

May 9, 1975
Business of Supply
can remain silent and hide all the facts from the people of Canada.

I should like to reply to the hon. member on that point of order. I am sitting in my place as a Minister of the Crown, not as a member of a party, yet the time I take is counted against the party on this side. I should like to give all the answers, but it is unfair that others should lose an opportunity to take part in asking questions. The hon. member for York-Simcoe urged me to reply right away to his questions. I did so, but I realized that the Liberal party would be deprived of time, and I respect the rule of the majority.

The minister's suggestion, if followed, would make these proceedings absolutely worthless. We have sat through debates with the Minister of Finance, for example, when his department was involved. He answered the questions we put to him, and there was no suggestion that somehow he was taking up the time of his hon. friends on that side of the House. I should like to see the minister answer some of the questions we have raised. He said he answered the questions I raised. I put 13 questions to him and he touched on two of them.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to know from you whether it is true that each time I speak the time allotted to members of the Liberal party is shortened accordingly?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: It doesn't really matter whose time the minister uses up. What is important is that the minister answer our questions. How could he possibly say he is not here as a party man. If he is not a Liberal, I have not seen a Liberal. Of course he is here as a party man, but he is also here as a member of the government appearing before the committee of the whole, the rules governing which have been worked out by his own House leader, the House leader of the NDP, myself, and others, because we wanted to see the thing work. The only way that it will work at all is if the minister exercises the responsibility that is his, rises in his place and answers the questions that have been put to him.
He has not got the guts.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
On point of order, Mr. Chairman, something has occurred this afternoon that was not contemplated when these new rules were designed and when they were discussed in committee. Some of us had always had the idea that when a minister rose to answer question put to him in these proceedings this was time that would not come out of the time allotted to the political party the minister represented, because he was answering as a Minister of the Crown. What has happened this afternoon is that members on this side of the House have not had an opportunity to speak because it has been considered by some members of the House that, in speaking, the minister has been a partisan of the Liberal party instead of speaking as a minister of the Crown.
It is clear that something has arisen which had not been contemplated. We do not dispute the right of the Chair to take the attitude it has, and we are not raising a point of

order from our side, but there will have to be discussions among the House leaders and others to decide how this procedure is to work. Mr. Speaker has made it clear, time and time again in the question period, that he is recognizing more members on this side than he has before. Therefore, if the Chair takes the attitude that the time taken by the minister is time taken from this side, then we will have to seek an accommodation to satisfy the members on this side, who are also members of parliament and have the right to participate in the proceedings of this House in the same way as any other elected member.
Perhaps the matter could be left where it is now and we will abide by the practice you have followed; but perhaps the committee would give the minister 20 minutes to sum up before the proceedings are concluded this afternoon.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The duty of the Chair is clearly that of balancing the time on both sides of the House. On the point of order that has been raised, members will recognize that time has been taken from the hon. member for Laurier who has been recognized. The hon. member for Laurier has the floor.

Mr. Chairman, twice you rendered a decision to the effect that when the estimates of the Treasury Board are examined, in view of the objectives set out in the Blue Book, almost any problem could be discussed. I do certainly not wish to-
A point of order, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Rocky Mountain is rising on a point of order.

I should like to have clarified, for my benefit and that of other members who want to have this proceeding make some sense and serve some purpose, whether it will be the intention of the minister responsible here, the President of the Treasury Board, to answer the questions put to him by members of the House, or whether he is going to use the lame excuse he just used, as another cover for not providing information to members of parliament. Is he going to get up and answer questions asked by my colleague from Grenville-Carleton, or is he going to continue to hide out?

Mr. Chairman, this morning I was very keen to get up and reply to the questions. I will take note of the questions, and if the House gives me time at the end I will try to reply. I felt it was a proper procedure to reply now, but in doing so, the rule, as it stands now, was depriving the majority of their time, and I decided I would not get up and deprive the majority of their rights as members of parliament.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Laurier.

In other words, you won't answer. You have absolute contempt for the House.
May 9, 1975

It seems, Mr. Chairman, that the opposition would like to muzzle the Liberals. I do not feel that this procedure is in order in a parliament, and when there is an indication that the Liberals wish to muzzle the opposition, then the members of the opposition grumble. Well I too am also going to grumble, because something had already been agreed upon almost ten minutes ago, and since then I have been interrupted.
A point of order, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for York-Simcoe on a point of order.

The minister made reference to what he understands is some rule governing these proceedings. I should like clarification. Is there any rule such as the minister has referred to, because the committee of the whole proceeding is absolutely useless if what the minister says is true? These government members can sandbag this thing until five o'clock.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They are members of parliament too.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There certainly is no such rule as that to which the hon. member for York-Simcoe has referred. There has been a decision from the Chair that it is standard practice in committee of the whole to balance the time on both sides of the House. That the Chair will endeavour to do. If the minister rises to respond he will, of course, be recognized. If he does not rise to respond on this side of the House, then another hon. member will be recognized, which is what has happened at the present time. The hon. member for Laurier has been recognized, and members have been eating into his time on various points of order.

Mr. Chairman, I hope that the interruptions I have been submitted to since you recognized me about 15 minutes ago will not be included in the time I was given to speak on the important matter of the Treasury Board's estimates.
As I said earlier, you did make a ruling that, when- [English]

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Go ahead and ask some questions.
Have you anything to say? If not, sit down because we have.
If you have something to say, say it.

Mr. Chairman, I have a lot to say, but even if there are very few opposition members here this afternoon, I think the matter we are considering is an important one. There are hardly ten of them, so I believe they are not entitled to ask me if I have something to say. They do not seem to have anything to say, except destructive criticisms. The member of the House asked whether I have anything to say. I do have a lot to say and I
Business of Supply
am going to take all my time to say it. I cannot see why they should continue to interrupt me in such a disgraceful way. But it is a habit that particular member has indulged in for some time and I cannot see where it will lead him. He may believe that his attitude will lead him to the leadership of the Progressive Conservative party, but I do not think it will. I believe that more qualified people might get the job.
Mr. Chairman, I would not like to be interrupted every other minute because I surely will have many difficulties to express what I have to say this afternoon about the Treasury Board.
As I said before I was interrupted many times, a ruling was made and sustained on two or three occasions, that, when one speaks about the objectives of the Treasury Board, one can speak about many matters. I am very glad-
Why don't you ask some questions?
If you have something to say I will sit down.

I have a number of questions to raise with the President of the Treasury Board. The hon. member has ceded his time to me. I am delighted to have that happen, and I am prepared to put my questions now to the President of the Treasury Board.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Laurier has the floor.

Mr. Chairman, it shows once more that he will surely not become the leader of the Progressive Conservatives.
As I was saying earlier, you made decisions that I consider very important as I am the chairman of a committee which is, as you know, the miscellaneous estimates committee and this, fortunately or unfortunately for the opposition, since 1968. From time to time, I had to make similar rulings as your own, Mr. Chairman, and the Liberal members of that committee often discussed my rulings on the relevance of the question put to ministers and you can be sure that I shall refer to your ruling when my own decisions will be discussed in committee.
As usual, it is not surprising, the opposition takes advantage-

Mr. Chairman, I must again rise on a point of order because the hon. member referred to the fact that your ruling would be remembered by him when he chairs one of his committees. We must get this proceeding into perspective. What is supposed to be happening today is in our opposition day the estimates have been brought back from a standing committee at which point we hope to have an opportunity to re-examine the situation and receive answers from the minister. In a standing committee there is never any suggestion when a minister is under questioning that his time should come out of the time of the Liberal members on that committee. They receive their

May 9, 1975
Business of Supply
relative pro rata time in the committee. To suggest that every time the minister stands up to answer a question from our side or from the government side the time should come from the Liberal side is totally wrong. I think it is an extremely alarming thing to hear from the chairman of one of the standing committees the suggestion that he will take this type of ruling back to the committee. The fact is that we should have the right to question the minister. Instead of loading the questions as I have to do by asking 13 of them I think he should be allowed to answer each question if we wish. I would ask that this would be reviewed and that we have a meaningful proceeding here. We have less than an hour and a half to go. We have questions we wish the minister to answer and at the present time it is obvious that we are going to be sandbagged up until five o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I rise on the same point of order, Mr. Chairman. If it is your ruling, and we are bound by that ruling for the balance of the afternoon, then may I say with the greatest respect that I hope you will place on the record that this is at least an experimental project. We are attempting to marry the old opposition day in the traditional sense with the committee of supply day of an even longer tradition. The marrying of this situation may contain some difficulties and there may have to be some discussions. If I may say so I would hope that you would at least indicate that your decision here today ought not to in any way bind the committee forever and that if it is to stand for today, at the very worst it should stand only for today and ought not to go any further.
I say this because there has been an honest attempt-I have said this to the government House leader and have said it on previous occasions-to do something to make this a meaningful procedure. When the hon. member for York-Simcoe stated as he did a few moments ago that the members of this House ought not to be impeded in terms of their time by virtue of an interjection or an answer to a question by the minister I think it is in the mind of every one of us that it should happen in this way and I hope you, Mr. Chairman, will not bind anyone occupying the chair in the sense of giving the hon. member for Laurier any comfort in his suggestion that he could take notice of this in committee as some sort of precedent. I do not think that should be the case.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that it was my point of order that initially fuelled this fire I might indicate I would join with the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton in his comment and hope that if there is to be some sort of consultation we would also consider my first point of order which was the subject matter and the length of the examination or debate which could take place.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The President of the Privy Council on the same point of order.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, I wish to support my colleague the acting House leader for the Conservative party, the Official Opposition, in saying I hope you will look upon this as an experimental day and an experimental procedure and avoid making any rulings until we have

had an opportunity to discuss these proposals. I have only one comment to make which I believe also should be borne in mind by those participating in the discussion this afternoon. The minister is placed in a rather awkward position when a member asks for answers to 13 questions and expects the minister to be able to answer them all in a very few minutes. I think this is one problem which has arisen. If this had not happened we might not have become involved in the difficulty we have this afternoon.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. Hon. members have referred to a decision from the Chair. I must say no such decision or ruling exists. The Chair simply declared that every effort would be made to apportion the time on both sides of the House. If the minister stands to be recognized, of course he will be recognized. So, there has been no ruling or decision made.
The standard practice in this committee is to apportion the time as equitably as possible. That responsibility which rests with the Chair is taken with the utmost seriousness. In the meantime the hon. member for Laurier has been recognized. He has had great difficulty in presenting his comments and time has been eaten up in this apportionment of time we are attempting to achieve.
The hon. member for Laurier.

Mr. Chairman, I was certainly not discussing your ruling and the translation may not have rendered exactly what I wished to express. Occasionally, as chairman of a very important committee of this House, the miscellaneous estimates committee, I must say that many members raise points of order concerning the relevance of questions.
I was saying that when we wish to discuss bilingualism, multiculturalism and other matters while reviewing the estimates of the Treasury Board, if members of the Opposition or Liberals are asking me similar question I might refer not necessarily to your ruling, but to the debate of this afternoon which I consider as a very valuable experience. I might occasionally refer to that debate to make a decision that might be favourable or unfavourable to the members asking the question depending on the problem raised. So, I would certainly not want in any way members of the opposition to think that I wanted to encroach upon their right to speak in committee. On the contrary, I think I am one of the committee chairmen who accept many questions that might otherwise be out of order. Then, of course, Mr. Chairman, it is a matter of experience.
I would like to come back to the problem before us this afternoon-the Treasury Board estimates.
It would seem the opposition is taking advantage of the new tentative set of rules now in the form of a nice white-cover book. It is a temporary set of rules for the House of Commons that was passed on March 24, 1975, but it would seem we will regret a lot having passed that new set of rules since the problems raised this afternoon do not seem to have been foreseen by the Committee on Procedure and Organization which drafted the new rules.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, the Treasury Board estimates were considered by the committee which I have had
May 9, 1975

the honour of chairing, as I said earlier, since 1968 in this House-they were considered on Monday, April 28, 1975. One can read the debates that took place on that occasion-quite interesting debates at that-in issue No. 29. Votes 1, 5, 10, 15 and 20 relating to the Treasury Board were considered. On that occasion, the minister responsible felt bound to reply to all the questions of the official opposition which was represented at that time especially by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), who is now away on official business, by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), who, of course is present as usual, and also by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling). As I said, we considered votes 1, 5, 10, 15 and 20.
It seemed then that the opposition was interested mostly in votes 5, 10 and 15 which I shall not read because it would take up some of my time, but they were explained by the minister, and I believe that the opposition should be satisfied with the replies given at the time by the President of the Treasury Board and his officials. However, under the new temporary rules in the House of Commons, it has been decided to discuss the Treasury Board issue further, and I understand this because, despite its comparatively low estimates compared with the total estimates, the Treasury Board is still one of the most important departments in the government, since it must select the programs and projects through which the government can achieve its goals as efficiently as possible, considering its priorities, and since it must also ensure that the departments and agencies use their manpower and equipment efficiently in implementing their programs and projects.
A while ago, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker)-and I understand him because this is the role of the opposition-made a rather scathing attack on the minister, but I have still to hear from the members of the opposition, of the official opposition or other opposition parties, positive suggestions and worthwhile recommendations likely to solve certain problems which now exist concerning the Treasury Board.
We all know that the hon. member for York-Simcoe makes scathing and partisan attacks, mostly unfounded, in committee, and he attempted during the study of the estimates-
