speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but the time allotted to him for participation in this debate has now expired.

Mr. Chairman, I want first to congratulate you for the manner in which you have directed the proceedings, difficult as that has been.
I would like to take two seconds time in reference to the rules. As I look around the House there are a few hon. members who were in the House when we used to meet and, under the old rules, go into committee of supply. Through you, Mr. Chairman, to the minister and to the House leaders who may be present, I say that, although I know each leader tried to bring about a compromise which would be somewhere between the new rules, which did not work at all, and the old rules, where there seemed to be too much time used in talk, the weakness in this new suggestion is that any minister can take the position that he is not going to answer questions, that he can sit out the

May 9, 1975
Business of Supply
storm of argument and questions, and therefore the opposition can never obtain any information.
I do not want to get into an argument with the minister; I simply point this out in an academic way. With the greatest of respect to everyone in the committee this afternoon, it becomes a total waste of time. The only suggestion I can think of, if we are not able to obtain answers, is to ask the House leaders to put their heads together again. I do not expect any minister to be a walking encyclopedia, because every department is large. There may be some information ministers may not be able to make available, but there should at least be an undertaking that at another time legitimate questions will be answered. There is always politics in the chamber, but ministers could come in at another time and make that information available.
Having said that I just want to say one other thing, which is of a political nature. When we went into the new rules brought about by closure, the Prime Minister had not even gone home for summer recess-I believe it was July-when I picked up the paper, and the Prime Minister was reported as saying that he had sure pulled the wool over the eyes of the opposition.
I believe that happened, but there is no use going back over old history. I see that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, a senior minister, is present. I ask all hon. members in this House, particularly those who have knowledge of the committee of the whole house, to consider this and to see whether we can devise a plan where we can ask legitimate questions and receive legitimate answers.
I want to discuss two or three points in reference to the minister's job. There may be something in the suggestion made by an hon. member that we cannot expect the President of the Treasury Board to answer for all departments, but I hope the other ministers will supply those answers.
The only growth in Canada is through real production and by trading our real production. The hon. member for York-Simcoe clearly pointed out that federal expenditures have increased 134.8 per cent from 1968 to 1974, from $12,229 million to $28,715 million. While the average weekly wage went from $88.19 in 1968 to $177.52 in 1974, an increase of only 101 per cent, the expenditures of the government went up 134 per cent. These figures spell inflation. Government expenditure is not real production or growth. When we get out of line that far, are we not fanning the flames of inflation?
I do not accept the minister's statement on several occasions that parliament approves the right of people in the public service to strike. I only differ with the minister academically, this is not a question of credibility. Particularly, I do not approve of certain areas of the public service having the right to strike; I have always said that if they are going to strike, let them all strike. I wish the Department of National Revenue would strike. People would be pretty happy about that.
What I am coming to now is under the jurisdiction of the minister, and I think it is very important. For 70 long days grain handlers and other people in the public service joined with the longshoremen in Vancouver while 55 ships waited in the ports. One could not even get into the ports

with a shoehorn, and nothing was done. Finally the government acted after 70 days and put those people back to work, but when they went back to work out of the pockets of western Canadian farmers $40 to $50 million went to demurrage charges.
We have now reached the point where men and women working in those kinds of industries, which are unique to the development and growth of Canada, and which we describe as essential services, must find some method other than the bargaining process to settle economic violence between management and labour. I was very pleased to hear the Prime Minister say something about that, and I can make it clear where I stand. I am prepared to stake my mandate in Calgary North or any other seat in Alberta on the belief that in the essential industries of this country the system we are using has failed, and it is feeding the fires of inflation across the nation.
I wish to point out to the minister how bad the situation is. The Minister of Justice responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board told farmers to produce more wheat in Saskatchewan and Alberta next year. Incidentally, grain is the second largest dollar producing industry in the country. Farmers are prepared to do as the minister has asked, but what happens now that quotas are going to be closed on May 15 and wheat is piled up on farms and in country elevators? Where will they store it if they do produce more grain? All of this has occurred as a result of disruption at the ports. The right hon. member for Prince Albert today pointed out that men and women are still on strike in the St. Lawrence ports. Western grain is being held up and is not going to the cattle industry, the poultry industry, and other industries important to the province of Quebec.
I want to ask the minister-and I wish I could get his ear instead of someone else talking to him-whether he does not feel that the time has come to have another system for settling this kind of economic violence. Second, has the time not come to enforce the law with regard to having men and women go back to work? If so, how is he going to do it?
Those are the two major questions, but I have one other I wish to put. This matter is not totally under the jurisdiction of his department, but it was raised by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, and it is in reference to the Calgary airport, which is a $40 million project. I have a wire in my hand from Darlington Haskins and Co. Ltd. and P.M. Dartnall Agencies, who point out that tenders were asked for certain jobs at that airport. These tenders were held 90 days from the time they were to be opened.
The contract was given to a company which they maintain is partly owned-I do not know whether this is correct but someone could check it out-by a former minister in the Liberal government. So they play ducks and drakes with companies in western Canada in order to break the tender rule, to give contracts to eastern Canada. I would ask them to check that. I do not think the minister can answer it today, but I hope that in the question period he will say that those jobs on the airport at Calgary will be properly tendered and there will be no hanky panky with Mr. Benson's Frontenac Company or any other Minister of the Crown.
May 9, 1975

These people maintain a Canadian company and have been in business since 1920. They say that the government architect in Calgary will confirm that their product was superior. They are a Canadian company but, due to hanky panky, a company from another part of Canada is to supply an inferior product at higher cost. That is what we are talking about, the right to tender when dealing with $40 million. The minister has the responsibility of administering the finances of all departments.
I have asked three questions, Mr. Chairman: first, about the violence on the docks; second, is the government going to pay back the farmers for their losses due to demurrage charges and third, is he going to get the men back to work on the St. Lawrence-is he going to force them back? I want to know about the contracts on the Calgary airport and the point raised by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton.
Those are my questions, Mr. Chairman, succinct and to the point.
The hon. member for Saint-Michel.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, if my time was to be taken out of that of the hon. member for Calgary North I will reply now, otherwise I will not reply until the end of the debate.
The hon. member for Saint-Michel.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether you were in the House when the former chairman took the chair but, as I understood his suggestion, although he did not make it a rule, this is pretty important to us and I hope you will hear me out. I am not trying to take up the time of the proceedings. I cut my time by half but I asked four important questions. The minister said he would answer me provided you did not take it out of the time of the government. I do not think we should. I think we should take it out of my time, and he has 10 or 15 minutes. I would like that exercised. You may look annoyed but, with the greatest respect, I am asking you because I did not take all my time and, secondly, I think he should answer those questions regardless of what rules you interpret again with the greatest respect to you.
The hon. member for Saint-Michel.

On a point of order I want your ruling and I am going to stand my ground. You can ask me to leave the House. I am a senior member. I have asked for the minister, and the minister is prepared to answer my questions out of my time. Are you ruling against me on my time?

President of the Treasury Board has indicated he would reply later on in the time that is allotted to the hon. member's questions. I think that is sufficient for the purpose of the questions put. I want to point out, with the greatest respect, that if we have enough people talking at a quarter to five the time you speak about becomes superfluous. There will be no time and I will get no answers to my questions. What I said earlier-if that is the kind of proceedings and we are trying to work it out-and I was very gentlemanly when I dealt with the rules-if that is the ruling, then you yourself have contributed to the kind of farce we have had this afternoon.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I would like to apologize to the hon. member for Alberta-whose name I forget-for having said that his constituency represents a double or a treble minority. I am a woman. I intend to talk about female employees in the public service. I am a French-Canadian, this is quite fashionable these days. Unfortunately, I have only two and a half years of service. This means that I am a fool, an idiot according to what I understood from his comments. This being said, there was such verbal inflation this afternoon that I nearly lost the thread of the questions I had intended to put to the hon. President of Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) about the public service. These questions dealt with what I thought was the principle of a fine public service in Canada.
The public service, to me, is something that provides a service of quality and shows an awareness to the needs of the public. Secondly, it is an available organization and thirdly, it is the embodiment of the government of this country, which should be demonstrated through simple justice for every member of the public service and it is with this point that I should like to deal in particular.
I was deeply struck, Mr. Chairman, by the speech of the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). I feel that this is an extraordinary example of chauvinism of all kinds and I have just understood why this side won the last election. That man is part of a "winners" and "losers" culture. He is a dollar man and a square foot man. Some are more square than others. I realized while listening to him-because he had a long creed in 13 points-that all that counts in life is money, not people. Therefore it is obvious that if he were a minister-he is eager to be a minister, at least Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce-he would never want to be Minister of Health and Social Welfare, because that is obviously too common.
It is certainly not chic to be a minister of people's problems. Besides it seemed to me that he would perhaps reduce the family allowances. Therefore he is interested in output, in the number of waste baskets a public servant is entitled to have in his office. As far as I could understand,

May 9, 1975
Business of Supply
it is for him a measure of efficiency and productivity in the public service. I am deeply disturbed because it is in a totally different way that I visualize that public service which includes almost 400,000 people.
I should like first to ask a question about one of the first minorities which need simple justice in that public service, namely the French-speaking Canadians. Over the two and half years I have been here, I have been hearing such nonsense on the French Canadians that I am beginning to ask myself serious questions. I should like to know how many bilingual jobs were added to those of the 53 per cent employees mentioned in his November 21, 1974 release.
I will not dwell any longer on the matter of French Canadian public servants except to mention that many of my constitutents and myself consider the bilingualism program in public service as a gift for English speaking Canadians because they have the opportunity to learn the second official language of the country during their work time at the expense of all Canadians. Many French Canadians suffered culturally from an impoverishment of the economical knowledge and of the management. Many wonder whether some kind of compensatory program should not be worked out on a sort of historical correction, offering to the French Canadians not English language courses, because the vast majority of them have to learn it painfully, but a management training program in order for them to have the same opportunities as English Canadians do have and for our public service to be really representative.
I would like to turn now to the bilingualism premium. In this week's newspapers the minister is reported as having made inconsistent statements. I could remember when I was a public servant that were forced by the pressure of the labour market to implement the bilingualism premium policy for secretaries and other related groups. I would like to know what philosophy he is in favour of so as to face the problem recently developed in Montreal in particular, concerning federal public servants who are using both languages at their own expenses because they learned them by themselves, and because their wage level is not quite much higher than the secretaries, and who wonder where is the equity in that bilingualism premium policy.
I will now turn to another issue. Nothing is easier for me, because I understand from the speeches ...

Mr. Chairman, as to the second item, I would like to say-I understand quite well that the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) should be particularly concerned at this point. His question is not complicated: he wants to make a separate mental category to know how much it costs to have French Canadians in the Public Service. Basically, that is the purpose I saw in his question. So, I suggest him to add another question: how much does it cost to give simple justice to women in the Public Service? We could perhaps in a year or so, with public opinion and the experiences of the opposition, ask how much it costs to have Indians in the Public Service. And then we could cover nearly everyone like that, at random. One day we will be left with a nice minority. How much does it cost to have Progressive Conservatives in the Public Service? I would like very much to know the cost of that, Mr. Chairman. It costs very much to have Progressive Conservatives in the Public Service.
Yes, yes.

Much too much. Progressive Conservatives in the Public Service are people who systematically prevent male and female Canadians from obtaining simple justice. They are the ones systematically sabotaging government programs, all programs that do not come under the dollar sign of the hon. member for York-Simcoe who operates on the basis of square footage and of the number of waste paper baskets in the offices of public servants.
That means that for him human beings, as he suggested, are not needed. That gentleman as well as the one I am talking to are people who work on the nineteenth century's principle of economic laissez-faire. It suits them because it is very simple. There is an expression for that- the law of the jungle, where the strongest wins. We French Canadians have indeed a very picturesque way of explaining it. It is an expression that I will not use because I am sure that the censorship will not allow it to pass.
I shall add that I consider the hon. member for York-Simcoe as a dinosaur, rather as representing dinosaurs and that he is an extraordinary prototype of the "winners" and "losers" culture. Mr. Chairman, I have been elected to care about the people who need and wish to be represented here in this House and surely not to make richer those who are already rich and one may wonder how they achieve their wealth.
With those republican words, I shall ask a few questions about a group that is not in fashion this year, the female public servants. Unfortunately, I heard the president of the Treasury Board say that we might be going backwards in that respect probably because of a few conservative minds that can still be found at certain levels of our public service. I am very concerned about it after the speeches made by the opposition today because if there is a priority presently in Canada, it is certainly to give justice to the employees. Therefore I should like to know how many women-and what percentage they represent-have been able to attend the courses recommended by the Royal Commission on the Status of Women and adopted by this government, which I commend it for, designed to help them to move from the ST or CR groups to the managerial
May 9, 1975

levels. I express here the problem of the promotion of women within an institution where a contemptible conservatism is still a blot on the escutcheon of the government.
Let me explain: there are bottlenecks at two levels and because of the old structures of our economy, they prevent women from having fair opportunities of equal promotion. First, secretaries and other related clerk categories do not manage to reach the managerial level, because their job is by nature or tradition entirely reserved for women.
Strange enough, I believe that it is exactly what happened between French Canadians and English Canadians in the public service. Up to March 1974, only 212 women and 47 men had been able to take advantage of the program I referred to. Of course, I do not object to male clerks having the opportunity to attend free courses and being promoted to the junior management level, but I know very well that this program has been initially designed for women, for a large group of women and that they are not fairly represented on a percentage basis.
Secondly, very few women have been able to reach higher positions; how and how many can and will reach the SX or the DM categories? This is the real issue of equal opportunities for men and women in the public service. I think that several deputy ministers appoint their assistant deputy ministers and directors.
It is practically obvious that if this system is not reviewed and is maintained, no woman will ever be able to accede to the position of director, assistant deputy minister and, naturally, deputy minister. Of course, all I have just said is based on the principle of equal ability. I am not concerned with that problem. When women reach a certain level, in general they are twice as qualified because they had to overcome obstacles which sometimes are legal, very often psychological, but nonetheless real, as we have seen this afternoon in the House while listening to the chauvinist remarks on the other side.
Concerning both aspects I have been dealing with, I would add that I am of the opinion that it is very important for the female public servant to have an opportunity to choose her career. In conclusion, I would ask the president of the Treasury Board whether he can give me the assurance that all these equal opportunities programs for female and male public servants will always be developed in close cooperation with the Advisory Board on the status of women.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I do not want to cut off the President of the Treasury Board. I just want to point out in fairly calm indignation that members on both sides have sat here trying to get involved in this committee of the whole dealing with supply.
I am one of the members who sat here when the old rules applied. In 1968 the new rules came in with closure and time limits. This whole thing has become a little farcical.

The point I want to make is that this is an opposition day based on supply. That is the prerogative of the opposition, not the prerogative of the hon. member for Saint-Michel and others.

In reply to the hon. member for York-Simcoe I have a few answers to give. He asked for the costs of furnishing Place Bell Canada. The cost was $490,000, something like $600-odd per capita. It is not that extravagant. The amount of space is 22,000 square feet, and we pay $5.97 per square foot in rental.
As for the cost of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, as usual the hon. member has not done his homework. What appears in the books this year is the cost of
May 9, 1975

the Unemployment Insurance Commission for last year; the cost this year will be found in the Blue Book of next year. So next year he will know. As far as the other questions are concerned, I shall look into them. If they are serious, and not too closely related to the furniture and so on, I will answer them. I will give all those answers by letter or by other means.
Turning to the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary North, of course I would like to have a better method of settling strikes, but I would point out to him that only 2 per cent of the collective agreements in the civil service since 1967 have been concluded following strikes; 98 per cent of the collective agreements between the government and its employees have been settled either by arbitration or through conciliation. The hon. member referred to the dockers. These are not civil servants. They work in the private sector and the Treasury Board has nothing to do with these disputes. I would like to debate that question, but I cannot do so now.
As to the question of compensation to farmers for the cost of demurrage incurred at Vancouver, the answer is no. I cannot be more precise. A further question was asked concerning the airport in Calgary. Tenders were called but only one bid was offered to the government which met all requirements, and we approved it. I might add that I have received a number of strong representations on the subject from members representing constituencies in Alberta- they were made in a very professional way; they have nothing in the back of their minds, but they wanted to have an answer. I gave them the answer. This expenditure of $40 million was approved by Treasury Board the other day. It was the only bid we had. Of course we wish we could have done better but we had no taker, and it was felt by the department that the bid was acceptable.
The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton is interested in bilingualism. He was complaining that figures as to cost are not easy to obtain. Well, the figures are in the Blue Book and I will, with the indulgence of the committee, read him some. Incidentally, the same question has been directed to me many times in the committee.
In the estimates of the Treasury Board, vote No. 1 official language branch, we find $1.3 million. Other figures are: Public Service bilingualism program, vote 15, $50 million; Department of the Secretary of State, bilingualism development branch, votes 5 and 10, $107.7 million; translation program, vote 30, $31.7 million; official languages minority group citizens program, votes 35 and 40 of those estimates, $3.6 million; under training, Public Service Commission, part of vote 115, $31 million; Urban Affairs, $300,000. The total is $225.5 million. There are some other items I cannot give to the House because I cannot go and count all the signs on all the doors of the toilets and the elevators and so on. Perhaps there were some costs involved there, but unfortunately I cannot give the figure. It would cost more to give the answer than the cost of putting on the signs.
The hon. member asked about bilingualism guidelines and about an incident which occurred this morning. I will have to give some thought to it-I am not in a position to give an explanation; these are term employees hired for four months only and we cannot send a man on a course for 12 months if he is to work for only four months.
Business of Supply
Six minutes is not very long in which to answer all these questions, but I am doing my best. The hon. member for Calgary North asked me another question-
I regret to interrupt the hon. minister but the time as allotted to him by agreement between the hon. members has expired.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, my questions will be very brief. Perhaps the minister will have more time in which to answer further questions when I am through.
Before I get to the matter which is closest to my heart, the subject of the federal nurses, I might be allowed to say a word with respect to the procedure presently being followed. There are not many members here who are familiar with the procedure followed when we dealt with estimates in the committee of the whole House. When that happened it was a day of accountability for Ministers of the Crown and members on the government side-and I know, because I have sat on that side and I remember how the whips applied the pressure-kept us quiet because they realized the minister concerned wanted to get his estimates through the committee. It developed into an opposition day; it was the opposition which was inquiring into the estimates, not members on the government side.
Try to transpose that system into the rules we are now following, under which the system is being used for the purpose of an allotted day. It won't work. If we are going to use the old system as a method of dealing with estimates, and call it an allotted day, new rules will have to be developed. The whole concept of an allotted day dealing with estimates loses all purpose if time is taken up by members of the House other than members of the opposition, whose duty it is to call the government to account.
I turn now to the further discharges this morning-I call them discharges even though they are not so called by the minister. I do not have my notes here now but my understanding is that out of 24 nurses at the National Defence hospital here in Ottawa, 17 have been told to go home because there was no work for them. They said to the hospital authorities, "Give us a certificate stating we have been laid off so we can apply for unemployment insurance." The hospital officials said no, they were not going to do that. They said, "You are on off duty status". The nurses maintain-and it seems logical to me-that there is no such thing. In effect it has every appearance of being a method to break down the nurses and to break the strike.
If the nurses are going to be laid off they should be told in order that they can have the same right as any other unemployed person to apply for unemployment insurance benefits. It is no excuse for adopting this tactic to say that there are not enough patients in the hospital and therefore their services are not required. My information, which could very well be inaccurate, is that this is being done by Treasury Board officials. Indeed, the name of Mr. Fother-gill has been mentioned in this connection. He is not here to answer for himself, but the minister is. I raise this because it is a very serious matter if the muscle of Treasury Board is being used in this fashion to break the strike.

Business of Supply
This morning I again raised the question of a COLA clause in the nurses' agreement. I know the conciliation board has recommended an increase, I think of 20 per cent, in the nurses' salaries, which just brings them level, for instance, with nurses in British Columbia. I understand the latter are already on the threshold of negotiating a new agreement, so that if the federal nurses accept the conciliation board report they will be behind again almost immediately, because the B.C. nurses are negotiating a better deal. I urgently suggest to the minister that he consider granting the nurses' request with respect to the inclusion of a COLA clause. If he does not, I think he will be a long way away from settling the strike. The minister has a minute left so I yield the floor to him.

Mr. Chairman, in regard to the National Defence Medical Centre, those people were sent home because there was no work for them. We have done the same thing in other cases; for example, the postal workers in Toronto. We are not under an obligation to keep people on the payroll if there is no work for them.
With regard to the COLA clause, although the nurses in British Columbia may be negotiating a new contract we have to live with the facts of today. We do use comparability. It was debated and there was a unanimous report. There was no discussion of a COLA clause, and probably because of the nature of the increase the conciliation board did not feel it should include a COLA clause.

As far as the hon. member for Saint-Michel (Miss Begin) is concerned, I am not in a position to give answers. She raised very valid questions on bilingualism and the status of women in the Public Service. Both these problems stand high in our priorities. Hopefully, we will be able to make significant progress in the years to come, and I expect that, as the situation of women within the Public Service, we will not be forced to give the same kind of answers as on the issue of bilingualism.

Mr. Chairman, before you see the clock, would the minister deal with the other serious aspect of the question that I raised regarding the muscle of Treasury Board being used deliberately for the purpose of breaking the strike of the nurses-that is to say, sending them home from work and not laying them off?
Mr. Chairman, the Treasury Board is an employer and it does these things in conjunction with the department. We are exercising the right of an employer as laid down in the legislation.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, without looking at the clock may I say I realize the minister did not have a chance of answering the first set of questions I put respecting the contract for advertising. I want to tell him that if he does not have time now he can write me.

I should like to make one specific comment, and that is that if someone starts to work on a contract that has not been approved by Treasury Board he does so at his own risk. I have seen cases where people took that chance and received no compensation at all.
